entries.title: Five Takeaways From the Commanders’ Preseason Win Over the Dolphins
entries.summary: With 29 key players on the sideline, Washington showcased its depth in a 20-7 victory.
entries.content:
Commanders running backs Kaytron Allen and Robert Henry Jr. combined for 160 rushing yards and the team’s defense stifled the Dolphins en route to a 20-7 win in the first of three preseason games.

The two teams met earlier this week for a joint practice in Ashburn. While Washington outplayed Miami during that session, Friday’s game was a different kind of matchup as both teams leaned heavily on their reserves — Washington held 29 players out of the contest.

Here are five takeaways from the night:

Ricky Barber and Byron Cowart can play. 

Baber, an undrafted free agent from 2025, and Cowart, a 30-year-old journeyman, best illustrated what the preseason is about: showcasing the less familiar players on the roster. Both defensive linemen put constant pressure on Miami’s quarterbacks. Barber tied for a team-high five tackles and added a sack and two quarterback hits, consistently putting his 295-pound frame in the Dolphins’ way.

Cowart, signed as a free agent on Tuesday, started off rough, whiffing on a sack of Quinn Ewers in the first quarter while committing a horsecollar penalty on the same play. But he came alive in the fourth quarter, causing pressure on the plays that caused quarterback Cam Miller to throw interceptions to linebacker Ale Kaho and safety Malik Spencer.

“Thats our motto: Attack the ball, get the ball,” Cowart said. “So to contribute to what we stand for here as a defense, what more can I do?”

The running back room just got interesting. 

Bill Croskey-Merritt and Rachaad White are virtual locks to make the final roster. Jeremy McNichols, who has missed practice recently with a quad injury, has been with the team the past two seasons and is lauded for his pass protection.

Allen, selected in the sixth round of April's draft, has typically spelled Croskey-Merritt and White in practice, but on Friday it was Henry, an undrafted rookie, who stole the show.

The University of Texas at San Antonio product showed elusiveness and the ability to change direction quickly on his way to 75 yards on just 12 carries. On Washington’s second possession of the second quarter, Henry took a handoff to the right before cutting back to the left for 15 yards. Two plays later he took another hand off to the right for a 22-yard touchdown run. Allen ended the day with 10 more yards than Henry, but it took nine more carries.

“The way I move, for sure,” Henry said when asked what he showed tonight. “I feel like I’m going to be able to express that more throughout the season but definitely the way I move. I feel like I’m twitchy, I got speed.”

Athan Kaliakmanis for QB3?

Sam Hartman has served as the Commanders’ third-string quarterback for the past two seasons, but he could be pushed for that spot this year. Kaliakmanis, drafted in the seventh round out of Rutgers, looked good in his first professional game. The stats won’t show it (6 of 10 for 87 yards and no touchdowns), but Kaliakmanis came in halfway through the third quarter and completed his first two passes of the day: a 16-yard out route to fellow rookie Antonio Williams and an 18-yard completion to tight end Colson Yankoff. On the same drive, Kaliakmanis threaded the needle between three defenders to find receiver Jacoby Jones, but Jones dropped the pass.

“I thought you’d see his arm strength come out a little bit, and it did, on some of the playaction plays,” coach Dan Quinn said of Kaliakmanis.

Hartman, who entered the game earlier than expected due to an injury to Marcus Mariota, was mostly inaccurate and had Washington’s lone interception after overthrowing Dyami Brown. But he did lead both of Washington’s touchdown drives.

The offensive line has growing pains. 

It’s hard to grade the offensive line’s performance Friday because the unit was missing left tackle Laremy Tunsil and center Nick Allegretti (injuries) and right guard Sam Cosmi and right tackle Josh Conerly Jr. (held out). That being said, the line did OK against Miami. It started off shaky, putting Mariota under pressure and not giving Allen much room to run. Guard Chris Paul let his defender slip through on a first quarter run and Allen was stuffed at the line of scrimmage. Later, tackle Andrew Wylie gave up a sack on a third down (Washington quarterbacks were sacked three times on the night). But as the game got going, the running backs found more space and the quarterbacks had the time to make some downfield throws.

Antonio Hamilton Sr. had a day. 

Hamilton epitomizes the “next play” mentality in football. The 11-year veteran defensive back had a tough start, giving up a one-handed catch to Miami rookie Caleb Douglas and committing pass interference in the process. But Hamilton shook that off and proceeded to have one of the more productive days on the defense: five tackles, one tackle for loss and one pass breakup. He also played on special teams, laying the hammer down on Dolphins return man Jalen Reagor in the second quarter.

“That’s going to happen,” Hamilton said of the Douglas catch. “You're going to give up a catch every now and then. They get paid, too. It’s just a next-play mentality as a DB.”

entries.title: Trump Administration Greenlights World Liberty Financial Bank Charter
entries.summary: The conditional approval comes soon after Trump reported more than $1.1 billion in crypto earnings in financial disclosures from last year.
entries.content:
The Trump administration conditionally approved a charter that would allow his family’s crypto venture to act like a bank, in an unprecedented arrangement that will enable the president’s family to pocket interest earned from corporate transactions.

World Liberty Financial, the stablecoin and trading platform co-founded by President Donald Trump and his three sons, was conditionally approved for a national trust bank charter on Friday. The move allows the cryptocurrency company to issue its dollar-backed stablecoin USD1 to institutional clients, convert other stablecoins to its own digital token and operate as a fiduciary for digital assets, according to a letter written by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, an independent Treasury Department bureau.

WLF’s conditional approval comes a little over a month after Trump reported more than $1.1 billion in crypto earnings in financial disclosures from last year, a sum that included more than $515 million from WLF token sales and $65 million from sales of equity in the venture’s holding company.

The OCC says final approval of WLF’s charter is contingent on the company meeting criteria including holding $20 million in high-quality, Tier 1 capital and a minimum of $10 million in liquid assets; informing the bureau before WLF appoints a senior executive officer; and retaining an internal auditor.

The national trust charter does not give WLF approval to operate a traditional bank’s full suite of banking and lending services, which would come with stricter oversight from the Federal Reserve. The OCC has granted conditional approvals to about a dozen crypto firms under the leadership of comptroller Jonathan Gould, who Trump nominated earlier this year.

WLF first applied for the charter on Jan. 5, the approval of which appeared a foregone conclusion to former staffers and industry watchers. An entity tied to the Trump family owns a 38% stake in the crypto company, which is partly managed by the president’s sons Eric Trump and Donald Trump, Jr. The president owns 70% of that LLC.

Senators recently punted a vote on the CLARITY Act, a cryptocurrency guardrails measure that has prompted additional discussion over the president’s ability to earn high figures from digital assets.

“This is the most brazen act of self-dealing our financial system has ever seen,” said Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts), the top Democrat on the Banking Committee, in a post to X following the conditional approval.

The preliminary approval letter acknowledged public comments expressing concern that Gould would not enforce regulations on WLF or would unfairly enforce regulations on competitors, and that the charter does not align with bureau precedent. Senior Deputy Comptroller Stephen A. Lybarger said in the letter that career OCC staff had reviewed and approved the application.

WLF has already come under scrutiny for conflicts of interest, including Trump’s October 2025 pardoning of Changpeng Zhao, whose company holds more than half of USD1s in circulation, and Emirati officials purchasing a 49% stake in the crypto firm days before the president’s inauguration.

entries.title: Data Centers Are Defining the Wisconsin Governor’s Race
entries.summary: The race could be a sign of Republicans’ ability to tap into growing national concerns about AI facilities.
entries.content:
Wisconsin hates data centers. Rep. Tom Tiffany, the state’s Republican gubernatorial nominee, wants voters to think his Democratic opponent doesn’t.

Tiffany entered the general governor’s race this week by claiming in a series of social media posts that Democratic candidate David Crowley wants to subsidize artificial intelligence facilities — even as the House Republican avoids supporting an all-out ban, instead calling for modest reforms and ending state subsidies for tech corporations.

Crowley says he doesn’t back a full moratorium on building AI facilities, instead supporting guardrails on the centers that already exist in the state. But Tiffany’s opening argument reflects a political reality: While data center protests are popping up and disrupting campaigns across the country, there are few places where the issue is currently as salient as it is in Wisconsin.

How the race plays out could be a sign of Republicans’ ability to tap into growing national concerns about the spread of AI facilities and their use of natural resources — a position that up until recently has been dominated by Democrats, largely due to the White House’s emphasis on developing AI in the U.S.

“I don’t believe him,” Kelly Gallaher, Racine Democratic Party chair, laughing while speaking about Tiffany’s promises to address the data center issue. “It was a politically expedient thing to say. … There’s nothing in his past that shows that he’s not amenable to influence from businesses or from the White House. So I just flat-out don’t believe him.”

It’s not surprising data centers have entered the general race so early, Gallaher said.

Developers have swarmed the state, including Microsoft’s recent investment of more than $7 billion in “the world’s most powerful AI data center” in Mount Pleasant, located in Gallaher’s Racine County.

Residents of the county she calls “Data Center Central” have voiced concerns about AI facilities for years — particularly after an infamous 2017 effort to build a Foxconn manufacturing plant there eventually failed, despite President Donald Trump’s heavy support at the time.

“We have seen this become a topic of conversation that really pre-exists this particular election,” Gallaher said. “It’s been building, and the candidates have been responsive to the talk on the ground, the temperature of the people who have really big concerns about them.”

On Friday, the Republican nominee posted a clip of Crowley speaking about an opportunity for the state to “become an AI and a data hub, not only for the entire country, but for the entire globe” before it flashes to Tiffany’s campaign logo.

In another shortened clip Tiffany posted on Thursday, Crowley says in an NBC interview that “data centers” are one way he differs from Francesca Hong, the progressive primary opponent he beat on Tuesday. Crowley at one point dropped out of the race before jumping back in nine days later, eventually beating Hong by roughly 4,000 votes.

The Republican’s campaign took the videos out of context, Crowley spokesperson Eddie Vale told NOTUS, chalking it up to “grasping at straws.” For instance, Tiffany’s NBC clip cuts out before Crowley finishes his thought: Hong supported a wide moratorium on the centers, while Crowley said he wants to not preempt economic development opportunities for communities.

“Tom Tiffany has not introduced any legislation to put any regulations on data centers across the country,” Crowley said in a statement Friday, blaming Wisconsin’s position on his Republican opponent and on Trump. “That is exactly what we need. That’s why we have a focus on creating state regulations to protect our communities across this country.”

The Tiffany campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

Tiffany had cast data centers as a farmland issue earlier in his campaign, tying the loss of valuable agricultural estate to tech developers. But after Tiffany handily won his primary race with more than 95% of the vote, this week’s immediate pivot to cast his opponent as welcoming of data centers also foreshadows an upcoming tight race the Republican hadn’t fully anticipated.

The House Republican had likely expected to face Hong in the general election after her surge in polling weeks ahead of Tuesday’s primary. Now that he’s running against a more centrist opponent in Crowley, Republicans are scrambling for a new playbook.

While only 5% of Wisconsin voters chose data centers as their most important issue in a July 22 poll from Marquette University Law School, more than three-quarters of respondents said the costs of data centers outweigh the benefits in the same survey — an increase from 55% last October.

But candidates across the state have launched a slate of anti-data center ads anyway. Combined, Wisconsin gubernatorial campaigns this year spent more than $1.7 million on broadcast ads that mentioned or focused on data centers, according to ad-tracking service AdImpact — comprising around 10% of total ad spending ahead of the state’s primaries.

The spending was helmed by two pro-Crowley PACs that dropped roughly $1.6 million on ads mentioning data centers, including spots that promoted how Crowley would “stand up to Trump and crack down on AI data centers” once elected.

The issue also stretched to other races this cycle: Democratic House nominee Rebecca Cooke spent $229,000 on an ad against Republican Rep. Derrick Van Orden, casting herself as a pro-moratorium candidate, while a handful of state legislative campaigns spent around $64,000 on broadcast ads about the centers.

Republicans like Tiffany opposing business development is a “new wrinkle” in state politics, said Charles Franklin, director of Marquette Law School Poll. While voters are most concerned about cost of living, some may connect data centers to electricity rates in wider affordability conversations, he said.

“Bottom line is, this will be the first campaign in which data centers will be an issue,” Franklin said in an email. “That will likely increase the salience. But if both candidates are calling for regulation and protecting consumers, it won’t be a sharp contrast between candidates.”

entries.title: DNC Adopts New Early State Presidential Primary Calendar
entries.summary: South Carolina will go first, followed by Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia.
entries.content:
AUSTIN, Texas — The Democratic National Committee on Saturday adopted a new early state calendar for the party’s 2028 presidential primary in a significant change that will have major implications for how Democrats pick their next White House nominee.

South Carolina will kick off the Democratic primary for only the second time, followed by Nevada and New Hampshire. New Mexico will be the fourth to hold a primary, marking the first time the state has been among the first in the country to vote.

Michigan and Virginia will round out the calendar as the fifth and sixth contests, respectively. Past primaries had included only four early contests.

DNC officials said the revamped early calendar better reflects the party’s diversity, giving Black and Latino voters a greater say in selecting the party’s leader.

“Our 2028 nominee, whoever they are, will have to earn this across the whole breadth of America,” DNC Chair Ken Martin said before the vote.

“No shortcuts, no coronation. You want to lead this party? You gotta earn it,” he said.

The new calendar was adopted by an overwhelming voice vote, with only a few audible dissents among the hundreds of DNC members gathered.

The adoption of a new calendar is a victory for Martin, who has faced a deluge of criticism over his leadership but has recently signaled that he is open to changes at the DNC.

Democrats adjusted their early primary calendar for the 2024 election as well, giving South Carolina the first primary and adding Michigan to the lineup in the fourth position.

The party’s last competitive presidential primary, in 2020, operated with a dramatically different map, eventually ending with Joe Biden winning the nomination. That year’s primary calendar started in Iowa, followed by New Hampshire, Nevada and South Carolina.

Iowa, whose 2020 caucuses were deemed a catastrophe, has since been removed from Democrats’ early state window. New Hampshire has been bumped back from second to third.

The DNC’s decision not to reinstall Iowa to the early window this year drew a sharp rebuke from Iowa Democratic Party Chair Rita Hart, who said the party is overlooking an entire region of the country and turning its back on a state that is on the verge of big Democratic victories in the November midterms.

“The 2028 calendar has no representation of states with a majority of Central or Mountain time zones, and no Midwest state is among the first four,” Hart said before Saturday’s vote, speaking to the committee in dissent.

Iowa Democrats had threatened to go rogue if the DNC didn’t include the state in its early lineup.

Saturday’s vote during the DNC’s general session was the culmination of a monthslong process to overhaul the party’s early state window. The new calendar was widely expected to be adopted after the influential Rules and Bylaws Committee recommended the list of early states last month.

The new schedule has South Carolina voting on Jan. 22, 2028, followed by Nevada on Feb. 1, New Hampshire on Feb. 8, New Mexico on Feb. 15, Michigan on Feb. 22, and Virginia on Feb. 29.
